content_list.content_text: French filmmaker Georges Méliès (1861-1938) was the first to explore this territory, seizing on the possibilities of slow motion, fast motion, superimposition, stop-motion animation, dissolves and all the other ingenious tricks cinema could play on audiences who were amazed, bewildered or terrified. As early as 1896, while Louis Lumière (1864-1948) — somber prose compared with Méliès's mischievous poetry — was showing his thrilling L'arrivée d'un train à La Ciotat (The Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat, 1895), Méliès was dazzling his patrons with Le manoir du diable (1896).

It is telling that the Lumière brothers started out as industrial chemists, whereas Méliès was a magician by profession. Yet, however imaginative they were, there was always something farcical about the French director's films, and it is hard to imagine many viewers were actually frightened or disturbed by them.

information.contentText: Méliès appears in the film as the apothecary and as his own duplicated head. To create the illusion of the expanding head, Méliès surrounded himself with a black background and used a specially built ramp to gradually move closer to the stationary camera. The head was then superimposed onto the rest of the image using the multiple exposure technique. The other special effects used are a mix of substitution and pyrotechnics.

content_list.content_text: Over the course of the 1910s, many of the classic fantasy creatures made their screen debut: Frankenstein in 1910, The Werewolf in 1913, among others. Vampires, however, had to wait until the following decade, with Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror (1922), directed by F. W. Murnau (1888-1931).

Witchcraft was another theme that fed the bubbling creativity of fantasy cinema. Danish director Benjamin Christensen (1879-1959) emigrated to Hollywood, but not before making his masterpiece: Häxan (1922), with its surreal blend of documentary and extraordinary fictional sequences. The film was a visceral attack on religious fanaticism, though it also found room for sardonic humor — especially when the director himself appears as Satan, playing the role stark naked. Most of Christensen's Hollywood films have unfortunately been lost.

information.contentText: With Christensen's meticulous re-creation of medieval scenes and its long production period, Häxan: Witchcraft Through the Ages was the most expensive Scandinavian silent film ever made, costing nearly two million Swedish kronor. Although it won acclaim in Denmark and Sweden, the film was banned in the United States and heavily censored in other countries for what were considered at the time graphic depictions of torture, nudity and sexual perversion. It is now considered Christensen's finest work.

content_list.content_text: Madmen, and especially mad scientists, were also guaranteed presences in early fantasy films — and they still are today. Abel Gance (1889-1981) made La folie du docteur Tube (The Madness of Dr. Tube, 1915), about a scientist who discovers how to change the appearance of people and objects, giving the director a cue to use distorting lenses freely.

The fantastic tales of Edgar Allan Poe were a popular source of adaptations, one of the first being Le système du docteur Goudron et du professeur Plume (Dr. Goudron's System, 1913), based on the short story The System of Doctor Tarr and Professor Fether, in which a visitor to an insane asylum has trouble telling the guards from the patients. The asylum would later reappear as the setting of Kurutta ippeji (A Page of Madness, 1926), a strikingly avant-garde drama by Japanese director Kinugasa Teinosuke (1896-1982) about a former sailor who works as a janitor at an asylum to be near his insane wife.

quote.quote: Ever since, I have never trusted the boundless power of an inhuman State gone mad.
quote.author: Hans Janowitz

content_list.content_text: With Das Cabinet des Dr. Caligari (The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, 1920), fantasy cinema took off — especially in postwar Germany. The film's distorted, Expressionist sets, which rejected any pretense of realism, the fragmented narrative, the hyper-stylized performances and the sense of paranoid insecurity came together to express the atmosphere of a defeated, traumatized nation, lacking confidence in its own identity and seeing enemies both within and without. The painted shadows of this film and of its silent-era successors seemed to anticipate — as Siegfried Kracauer and other critics pointed out — the shadows that would deepen in the German collective psyche in the years to come.

It is no surprise that Death, whether in the form of the Grim Reaper himself or of his various demonic incarnations, dominated German cinema during its most creative period. Released the same year Nosferatu appeared, Der müde Tod (Destiny, 1921), by Fritz Lang, shows Death offering a young woman, whose fiancé he has taken, three chances to bring him back. But the stories Death shows her — set in the Baghdad of the caliphs, Renaissance Venice and a fairy-tale China — only prove the impossibility of saving a doomed life, and in the end the bride agrees to die so she can be reunited with her beloved.

information.contentTitle: The Phantom of the Opera - Ball Scene
information.contentText: Lon Chaney's revolutionary makeup in The Phantom of the Opera was designed to resemble a human skull.

content_list.content_text: Throughout the rich range of fantasy films from the German silent era there is a sense that dark forces are taking over, that things are coming unhinged and sliding inexorably toward a fatal abyss — once again making the comparison with the nightmare that would soon engulf the country inevitable. Not that German cinema held a monopoly on the fantastic during that period. Hollywood produced a series of films starring the chameleonic Lon Chaney, who established himself as one of the most powerful actors of his time. In one of his most memorable performances, Chaney played the disfigured Phantom in The Phantom of the Opera (1925).

Although these Hollywood fantasies featured extraordinary morbid elements, they were essentially grotesque stories set in realistic environments. They lack the distressing sense of an entire world out of joint that was so strong in German cinema of the period. A rare exception was The Man Who Laughs (1928), directed by Paul Leni and starring Conrad Veidt, who plays Gwynplaine, the son of a decadent English nobleman who had offended King James II. On the monarch's orders, Gwynplaine is disfigured, left with a permanent gash of a grin on his face.

information.contentTitle: Scene from The Man Who Laughs
information.contentText: History's first fiction film has always been a rich source of inspiration. Jack Nicholson's Joker in Tim Burton's 1989 Batman is a tribute to Cesar Romero's villain, but recalls the caricatured Freder (Gustav Fröhlich). Likewise, Dr. Rotwang (Rudolf Klein-Rogge) inspired Doc Brown (Christopher Lloyd) in Back to the Future, and the "Creepy Thin Man" villain in Charlie's Angels (2000) is inspired by "The Thin Man" from the German film.

content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Philip Kemp, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

content_list.content_text: German Expressionism is one of the most recognized styles of silent film, although it is sometimes hard to define. The Expressionist movement in the arts first emerged in poetry and painting in the early 20th century, also influencing theater, architecture and, naturally, cinema, especially after World War I (1914 to 1918).

information.contentText: History's first fiction film has always been a rich source of inspiration. Jack Nicholson's Joker in Tim Burton's 1989 Batman is a tribute to Cesar Romero's villain, but recalls the caricatured Freder (Gustav Fröhlich). Likewise, Dr. Rotwang (Rudolf Klein-Rogge) inspired Doc Brown (Christopher Lloyd) in Back to the Future (1985), and the "Creepy Thin Man" villain in Charlie's Angels (2000) is inspired by "The Thin Man" from the German film.

content_list.content_text: What Expressionism sought was a subjective representation of the world, one capable of revealing the anguish of human existence through distorted images far removed from reality, evoking nightmares. These concepts originated, in part, in German Romanticism.

With its use of shadows and contrasts, stories tackling unsettling themes, and exaggerated sets, makeup and costumes, German silent film of the 1920s laid the foundations for two major genres of modern cinema: the horror film and film noir.

quote.quote: I believe that the films of the future will use more and more of these 'camera angles' or, as I prefer to call them, these 'dramatic angles'. They help cinematic thinking
quote.author: F.W. Murnau

content_list.content_text: Like Expressionist paintings, the films of this period sought to address the personal and subjective experiences of human beings. In cinema, this trait is most particularly associated with unrealistic sets, steep angles and striking shadows that heighten the film's atmosphere.

The Italian term chiaroscuro (light-dark) is often used to describe this kind of high-contrast cinematography between light and darkness, but German critic Lotte H. Eisner, author of The Haunted Screen (1952), preferred an expression from her own language: helldunkel, which she defined as "a kind of twilight of the German soul, expressing itself in gloomy and enigmatic interiors or in hazy and insubstantial landscapes."

To make up for the lack of big budgets, the early Expressionist films used unrealistic sets, with designs painted on the walls and floors to represent lights, shadows and objects. The stories and narratives generally dealt with madness, insanity, betrayal and other existential themes brought to the surface by the traumatic experiences of World War I.

information.contentText: The film's sets were made of paper, with the shadows painted on them.

content_list.content_text: This dark, melancholy school of filmmaking was eventually carried over to the United States later on, when the Nazis seized power and many German filmmakers were forced to emigrate to Hollywood. These artists realized that the American studios were willing to welcome them, and several German directors and camera operators found success in the country, producing Hollywood films that left their mark on cinema as a whole. According to theorist Siegfried Kracauer, author of the book From Caligari to Hitler (1947), German cinema of the Golden Age — that is, the silent films made before Hitler's takeover of the country and the subsequent rise of the Third Reich — already showed signs that Nazi Germany was inevitable.

Among the most emblematic films of German Expressionism, The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari certainly deserves special mention. The film is famous for its harrowing atmosphere and macabre story, in which the character Francis tries to solve a series of murders he suspects are the work of a hypnotist, Dr. Caligari, and his somnambulist accomplice, Cesare. Many have interpreted the feature as an allegory of World War I, in which Cesare represented the innocent soldiers driven to crime by the manipulation of an authoritarian and abusive government (represented by Caligari).

Another highly representative film of German Expressionism was Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror, by F.W. Murnau. Although it used many real locations, which was uncommon in films of the time, the film builds despair and anguish in an escalating, frightening way. Murnau turns the familiar into something strange, giving Expressionist touches to real-life landscapes, which gradually carries the viewer from reality into nightmare. The vampire, who symbolizes the inevitability of death, is a loose adaptation of Bram Stoker's Dracula.

content_list.title: From the Page to the Screen
content_list.description:
Henrik Galeen's screenplay for Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror largely follows the plot of Bram Stoker's classic vampire novel Dracula (1897), although it simplifies the story and eliminates or sidelines a number of characters.

Jonathan Harker, the young hero, becomes Hutter; Professor Van Helsing, Dracula's powerful antagonist, is reduced to the useless Professor Bulwer. The theme of female sacrifice in the film (Ellen, Hutter's wife, gives herself to the vampire in order to destroy him) is not in the novel. The setting also changes: Whitby becomes the fictional Baltic port of "Wisborg." And Dracula himself becomes "Count Orlok," supposedly to disguise the fact that the filmmakers had used Stoker's plot without permission.

If that was the reason, it didn't work: Stoker's family won a copyright infringement lawsuit, and a court order required that all copies of the film be destroyed. Prana studios (a Sanskrit word meaning "life force") went bankrupt, making Nosferatu its first and only release.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Philip Kemp, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

content_list.content_text: Metropolis (1927), by Fritz Lang, is also considered one of the most famous films of Expressionism and of silent film as a whole. The feature blends Gothic elements with a futuristic aesthetic that still inspires the science fiction genre today. With its extreme vision of a society driven by class struggle, with the rich living at the brightly lit top of the city and the poor below, in the shadows, the film reveals the economic inequalities of Weimar Republic Germany, blending personal anguish with social critique. The crowd of workers itself is an essential part of the film's visual aesthetic, moving in a symmetrical, mechanical way, like the giant machine they serve.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the article Expressionismo Alemão (German Expressionism), by Katia Kreutz

movies.title: Nosferatu the Vampyre
movies.overview: Jonathan Harker, a real estate agent, goes to Transylvania to visit the mysterious Count Dracula and formalize the purchase of a property in Wismar. Once Jonathan is caught under his evil spell, Dracula travels to Wismar where he meets the beautiful Lucy, Jonathan's wife, while a plague spreads through the town, now ruled by death.

movies.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari
movies.overview: Francis, a young man, recalls in his memory the horrible experiences he and his fiancée Jane recently went through. Francis and his friend Alan visit The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, an exhibit where the mysterious doctor shows the somnambulist Cesare, and awakens him for some moments from his death-like sleep.

movies.title: The Haunted Castle
movies.overview: Le Manoir du diable or The House of the Devil, released in the United States as The Haunted Castle and in Britain as The Devil's Castle, is an 1896 French short silent film directed by Georges Méliès. The film tells the story of an encounter with the Devil and various attendant phantoms. It is intended to evoke amusement and wonder from its audiences, rather than fear. However, because of its themes and characters, it has been considered to technically be the first horror film, as well as potentially the first vampire film.  The film opens with a large bat flying into a medieval castle, circling a room, and then suddenly changing into the Devil. Producing a cauldron, Mephistopheles conjures up a young girl and various supernatural creatures in an effort to scare two cavaliers, eventually succeeding in causing one to flee. Ultimately the remaining cavalier is confronted face-to-face by the Devil before reaching for and brandishing a large crucifix, which causes the Devil to vanish.

movies.title: Frankenstein
movies.overview: Frankenstein, a young medical student, trying to create the perfect human being, instead creates a misshapen monster. Made ill by what he has done, Frankenstein is comforted by his fiancée; but on his wedding night he is visited by the monster.

movies.title: Häxan
movies.overview: Grave robbing, torture, possessed nuns, and a satanic Sabbath: Benjamin Christensen's legendary film uses a series of dramatic vignettes to explore the scientific hypothesis that the witches of the Middle Ages suffered the same hysteria as turn-of-the-century psychiatric patients. But the film itself is far from serious-- instead it's a witches' brew of the scary, gross, and darkly humorous.

movies.title: The Madness of Dr. Tube
movies.overview: A scientist develops a powder that he believes will have the effect of distorting reality for those who take it. To test its effect tries it out on his assistant, a dog, himself and two young couples.

movies.title: The Phantom of the Opera
movies.overview: A grotesquely disfigured composer known as "The Phantom" haunts Paris' opera house, where he's secretly grooming Christine Daae to be an opera diva. Luring her to his remote underground lair, The Phantom declares his love. But Christine loves Raoul de Chagny and plans to elope with him. When The Phantom learns this, he abducts Christine.

movies.title: The Man Who Laughs
movies.overview: Gwynplaine, son of Lord Clancharlie, has a permanent smile carved on his face by the King, in revenge for Gwynplaine's father's treachery. Gwynplaine is adopted by a travelling showman and becomes a popular idol. He falls in love with the blind Dea. The king dies, and his evil jester tries to destroy or corrupt Gwynplaine.
